questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the winner under a plurality rule
questions.stem: In a chart note, Dr Halem records that a patient's district returned one representative and three candidates contested it, with the leader taking thirty-six percent of the vote.

options.text: The candidate with the most votes wins the seat, even without a majority.
No representative is returned until one candidate passes fifty percent.
options.misconception: applies a majority threshold to a plurality rule

options.text: The seat goes to the candidate with the largest membership roll.
options.misconception: confuses votes received with party membership size

options.text: A second round is required because no candidate won a majority.
options.misconception: assumes a runoff is always needed in this system

questions.explanation: Under plurality the highest vote-getter wins the seat regardless of majority, so a three-way split still returns a member. A second round and membership counts belong to other arrangements.
questions.hint: Check the rule for a split vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how proportional allocation converts votes into seats

stimulus.body: The bulletin for the district notes that seats are assigned across the whole region in proportion to the votes each party received. A party with eighteen percent of the vote received eighteen seats in a chamber of one hundred. The bulletin adds that two seats were assigned on the basis of remainders after the main distribution.

questions.stem: Based on the bulletin, which description of the seat allocation is correct?

options.text: Seats are distributed by constituency, so each party keeps what it wins locally.
options.misconception: confuses proportional allocation with constituency results

options.text: Seats follow the national vote share, with remainders filling the last places.
Seats are shared equally among the parties that cleared the threshold.
options.misconception: describes an equal split rather than a proportional one

options.text: Seats are assigned by agreement among the parties after the count.
options.misconception: describes negotiated allocation rather than the stated rule

questions.explanation: Proportional allocation ties seats to the national vote share, so eighteen percent of the vote yields eighteen of one hundred seats. The last places go to the largest remainders, a mechanical step, not a negotiated one.
questions.hint: Compare the vote share with the seat share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a disproportional outcome in a seat table
questions.stem: A case conference notes that a party with thirty-one percent of the vote holds thirty-eight of one hundred seats, while a party with twenty-nine percent holds twenty-two seats.

options.text: The result is proportional, because both parties are under half the vote.
options.misconception: equates being below half with proportionality

options.text: The result cannot be judged without knowing the size of the chamber.
options.misconception: claims disproportionality needs a figure the note supplies

options.text: The result is disproportional, because seat shares diverge from vote shares.
The result is proportional, because the larger party gained fewer than it wanted.
options.misconception: confuses dissatisfaction with a seat-vote mismatch

questions.explanation: Thirty-eight seats against a thirty-one percent vote is over-representation, while the other party is under-represented. Proportionality requires the two shares to match, not merely to fall under half.
questions.hint: Compare the two shares for each party.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why plurality systems tend towards few effective parties
questions.stem: The clinic's civic note must explain why district-based plurality elections tend to produce only two effective parties.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that plurality rewards concentrated support. A party with voters spread thinly across many districts wins few seats, because it rarely finishes first anywhere, while a party whose support is clustered wins seats in proportion to the size of its strongholds. Once the second pattern is rewarded, parties in between have little reason to exist, because merging with one of the two survivors would raise their chances of topping the poll, and voters who fear a close runoff have an incentive to concentrate on a single candidate. The result is a two-party pattern, and it holds wherever districts elect a single member by first past the post.

questions.explanation: Plurality rewards concentrated support, so thin national support wins few seats and the middle of the party spectrum is squeezed out. Voters and parties alike gain from concentrating on fewer contenders.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of support the rule rewards.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how governments are formed after a fragmented election
questions.stem: A clinic meeting note records that after the last election no party held more than thirty-four of one hundred seats.

options.text: A single party will govern, because the largest party wins the count.
options.misconception: assumes the largest party governs without any majority

options.text: The president will appoint a government from the largest party alone.
options.misconception: assumes a presidential appointment route where none is described

options.text: A coalition will form, because no party reached fifty percent of seats.
options.misconception: treats the absence of a party majority as sufficient for a coalition

options.text: A government will form only if parties that can combine reach a majority.

questions.explanation: With no party holding a majority, a government can only be formed by parties that together reach one, and the chamber arithmetic decides who is needed. The largest party alone has no claim to govern.
questions.hint: Ask which parties can combine.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an electoral threshold

stimulus.body: The intake note records that the regional election uses proportional allocation and excludes parties that polled less than five percent, citing the difficulty of governing with a large number of tiny groups. The note observes that two parties with four and four and a half percent of the vote won no seats at all, while the party with five and a half percent won four.

questions.stem: What does the intake note show about the effect of the threshold rule?

options.text: The threshold excludes small parties and reduces the number of represented groups.
The threshold has no effect, since excluded parties keep their votes elsewhere.
options.misconception: believes excluded votes are redistributed to other parties

options.text: The threshold increases fragmentation by admitting every small party to the chamber.
options.misconception: reverses the effect of a threshold on the number of parties

options.text: The threshold transfers votes from large parties to the excluded ones.
options.misconception: imagines a transfer mechanism that the note does not describe

questions.explanation: A five percent threshold excluded the two parties below it while admitting the party just above it, so the rule reduces the number of groups holding seats. Excluded votes are not redistributed, and fragmentation falls rather than rises.
questions.hint: Compare who won seats and who did not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of a dominant-party system
questions.stem: A referral note describes a country where one party has won every election for thirty years, the opposition still fields candidates, and no party other than the leader has been allowed to register.

options.text: A two-party democracy, because an opposition contests every election.
options.misconception: treats the presence of an opposition as real competition

options.text: A hybrid regime, because some competition survives between elections.
options.misconception: ignores the registration ban that removes genuine competition

options.text: An authoritarian regime, because no rival may register to contest.
A dominant-party system, because one party wins every election.
options.misconception: assumes a long winning streak proves a dominant-party system

questions.explanation: A dominant-party system still allows rivals to compete; here registration is barred, so competition has been removed rather than merely unbalanced. A long winning streak alone would suggest a dominant-party system.
questions.hint: Ask whether rivals can actually register.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess how electoral rules shape party fragmentation
questions.stem: A second civic note must explain why two democracies using different electoral rules can show very different numbers of effective parties.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that the number of effective parties is shaped by the electoral rule rather than by social cleavages alone. Under a single-member plurality rule, parties need concentrated support to win seats, and the rule rewards consolidation, so two large parties are typical. Under proportional allocation, votes are converted into seats across the whole country, so a party with a modest but nationally spread support base can win seats in the same proportion as its vote, which keeps more parties viable and produces a more fragmented chamber. The note should add that thresholds then trim the tail further, so the rules interact rather than working one at a time.

questions.explanation: Plurality rewards concentrated support and consolidation, while proportional allocation rewards spread support and sustains more parties. Thresholds trim the tail again, so rules interact.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of support each rule rewards.

questions.learningObjective: Define civil society and distinguish it from the state

options.text: Civil society, because it is an organised group outside state and market.
A political party, because it campaigns for policy change in public.
options.misconception: equates campaigning for policy with party organisation

options.text: A government body, because it addresses a public policy issue.
options.misconception: confuses a non-state group with a public authority

options.text: A business interest, because it is organised and seeks influence.
options.misconception: treats any organised influence-seeking body as a business

questions.explanation: Civil society covers organised groups that sit outside the state and the market, such as associations and charities. Whether a group campaigns for policy does not make it a party, and it is neither a public body nor a business.
questions.hint: Ask where the group sits relative to the state.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish political parties from other organised groups

stimulus.body: The minutes record that a farming association has announced it will contest the next election in three districts, that it will publish a programme and nominate candidates, and that it will seek to form alliances with other organisations. The chair insists the group has existed for forty years and already has a broad membership.

questions.stem: Do the minutes describe a political party under the usual definition?

options.text: No, because a group must hold seats to count as a political party.
options.misconception: requires winning seats before a group can be a party

options.text: No, because the association is a farming body rather than a party.
options.misconception: assumes a policy focus prevents electoral organisation

options.text: Yes, because the association has a long history and broad membership.
options.misconception: treats age and membership as the decisive tests

options.text: Yes, because it contests elections and pursues electoral aims.

questions.explanation: Political parties are organisations that contest elections and pursue office, and this group does both. Long history and broad membership are supporting facts, not the defining test, and losing seats would not change that.
questions.hint: Ask whether the group contests elections for office.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the winner under a plurality rule
questions.stem: A discharge summary compares two districts, one where the winner took forty-one percent and another where the winner took forty-nine percent.

options.text: Only the second district is valid, because a majority was needed there.
options.misconception: imports a majority threshold into a plurality rule

options.text: The first district was miscounted, since forty-one percent is too low.
options.misconception: treats a weak plurality as evidence of miscounting

options.text: Both seats are valid, because plurality accepts the highest vote share.
The first district must be rerun, since the margin was too narrow.
options.misconception: assumes a rerun is required when the margin is narrow

questions.explanation: Plurality asks only who polled most votes, so winners at forty-one and forty-nine percent are equally valid. The size of the winning margin bears on the strength of the mandate, not on whether the result stands.
questions.hint: Compare validity, not margin.

questions.stem: A clinic bulletin explains that in the regional chamber a party's seat entitlement is calculated by multiplying its vote share by the total number of seats.

options.text: That is the proportional formula, converting votes into an exact seat entitlement.
That is the plurality formula, where the largest vote share wins the seat.
options.misconception: labels a proportional formula as a plurality rule

options.text: That is the threshold formula, since it removes the smallest parties.
options.misconception: mistakes an allocation step for the exclusion rule

options.text: That is the remainder formula, which decides the final seats.
options.misconception: mistakes the entitlement step for the remainder step

questions.explanation: Multiplying vote share by the number of seats is the entitlement step in proportional allocation, before remainders are distributed. Plurality needs no such multiplication, and thresholds and remainders are separate stages.
questions.hint: Name the step being described.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise a disproportional outcome in a seat table

stimulus.body: The case note records that in a hundred-seat chamber one party won forty-two seats on thirty-five percent of the vote, and that a second party won thirty-one seats on thirty-three percent. A third party won nineteen seats on twenty-nine percent. The note adds that the first two parties together form a governing majority.

questions.stem: What does the case note indicate about the proportionality of the result?

options.text: The result is proportional, because the seat shares add up to one hundred.
options.misconception: treats the total of seats as evidence of proportionality

options.text: The result is mildly disproportional, since seat shares exceed vote shares.
The result is proportional, because no single party holds a majority.
options.misconception: confuses the absence of a majority with proportionality

options.text: The result cannot be assessed, because vote shares are not seat shares.
options.misconception: claims proportionality cannot be assessed from matched figures

questions.explanation: Seat shares of forty-two and thirty-one exceed vote shares of thirty-five and thirty-three, so the result leans towards the first party. That is mild disproportionality, and it is what produced the governing majority.
questions.hint: Compare each seat share with its vote share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why plurality systems tend towards few effective parties
questions.stem: The note must set out why voters in single-member districts tend to concentrate their support on one candidate.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that in a single-member district the prize is one seat, and a candidate polling around a third of the vote may still lose to a rival polling a little more. Voters who fear wasting their vote on a candidate who will come second therefore have a reason to back the one most likely to win, and once that habit spreads across districts the opposition loses the seats where it is strongest and the overall pattern narrows to two viable parties. The note should add the qualification that this pressure is weaker where a second round gives a runner-up a fresh chance and where voters have a transferable vote they can use for a compromise candidate.

questions.explanation: Because only one candidate wins a district, a plurality winner may need far less than half the vote, so voters concentrate to avoid wasting their vote. The pressure weakens where runoffs or transferable votes apply.
questions.hint: Think about the risk of voting for second place.

options.text: A coalition of the two can govern, because their seats exceed a majority.
No government is possible, because no party holds a majority.
options.misconception: misses the possibility of a coalition reaching a majority

options.text: An election must be repeated, because a majority was not achieved.
options.misconception: assumes a repeat poll is required after a fragmented result

questions.explanation: With thirty-nine and twenty-two seats the two partners together control sixty-one of one hundred, so they can form a government without any single party holding a majority. The largest party alone could not, because thirty-nine is short of fifty.
questions.hint: Add the seats and check the majority.

questions.stem: A clinic notice explains that parties polling less than five percent of the national vote receive no seats under the regional rule.

options.text: The rule is a district system, since seats depend on local results.
options.misconception: confuses a vote threshold with a district system

options.text: The rule is a threshold of inclusion, since all parties are rewarded.
options.misconception: reverses the meaning of a threshold rule

options.text: The rule is an exclusion threshold applied after the vote.
The rule is a majority requirement for forming a government.
options.misconception: confuses a seat threshold with a government threshold

questions.explanation: A minimum vote share below which a party wins no seats is an exclusion threshold. It filters the result after the count and is separate both from how seats are won and from the arithmetic of forming a majority.
questions.hint: Ask what happens below the stated figure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of a dominant-party system
questions.stem: A reviewer claims that a country with one party winning every election for decades but with real opposition parties contesting freely must be authoritarian.

options.text: The claim holds, because uninterrupted dominance rules out democracy.
options.misconception: treats a long winning streak as proof of authoritarianism

options.text: The claim holds, because dominant parties always suppress rivals.
options.misconception: assumes dominance always involves suppression of rivals

options.text: The claim fails, because no party ever wins every election in a democracy.
options.misconception: invents a rule that democracies must rotate winners

options.text: The claim fails, because dominance with free rivals is a dominant-party system.

questions.explanation: A dominant-party system is one in which one party wins most elections while genuine rivals remain free to compete, which is not the same as authoritarian rule. Dominance becomes evidence of authoritarianism only when competition is blocked.
questions.hint: Ask whether rivals can compete freely.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess how electoral rules shape party fragmentation
questions.stem: The note must compare how a plurality district system and a proportional list system reward different kinds of parties.

answer.exemplar: The note should compare the incentives each rule creates. A plurality district rule gives a seat to whoever finishes first in one geographical area, so a party that is strong everywhere or strong enough in a few districts is rewarded, while a party with modest, evenly spread support can win nothing at all. A proportional list rule computes entitlement from the national vote, so a party with modest spread support gains seats in line with its share, and a party that concentrates its support loses the reward for concentration. The note should conclude that neither rule is neutral, since each favours a different kind of party and therefore a different party system.

questions.explanation: Plurality rewards concentrated support and punishes spread support, while proportional allocation rewards even spread. Neither rule is neutral, since each favours a different kind of party.
questions.hint: Ask which support pattern each rule rewards.

options.misconception: assumes a shared interest makes a body a trade association

questions.explanation: An independent group that campaigns on a public issue but seeks no office is part of civil society. Campaigning on policy is not the same as organising to contest elections, and the group is neither an authority nor a commercial body.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how governments are formed after a fragmented election
questions.stem: The civic note must explain why the size of the largest party shapes the bargaining position of the others after an election.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that in a fragmented chamber the largest party's leverage comes from being the only plausible route to a majority. If it holds thirty-eight seats and the next party holds twenty-two, then a partner joining the largest brings it past the halfway mark, while a partner joining the second may still fall short, so the largest can often dictate the terms of an agreement. The note should add that this leverage weakens when several mid-sized parties hold similar numbers, because then the largest needs more partners and each of them can negotiate from a stronger position, and that the arithmetic of remainders can shift these balances by a seat or two.

questions.explanation: The largest party can dictate terms when only it can reach a majority with one partner, because smaller parties depend on it. When several mid-sized parties are similar, the largest must court more partners and each has more leverage.
questions.hint: Ask who needs whom more.

options.misconception: explains the pattern by district size rather than the rule

options.text: Because plurality rewards concentrated support, smaller parties are squeezed out.

options.text: Because the electoral threshold excludes every third party.
options.misconception: assumes a threshold that single-member districts do not have

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of a dominant-party system

stimulus.body: The minutes record that the largest party has won every election since the system changed, with vote shares between thirty-four and forty-one percent, while three opposition parties have contested every election and together hold a quarter of the seats. The chair notes that turnout has fallen slightly and that the largest party has campaigned on welfare and regional development issues.

questions.stem: What does the minutes suggest about the party system described?

options.text: A dominant-party system, where one party leads while rivals remain free.
An authoritarian regime, because one party always wins the election.
options.misconception: treats a winning streak as proof of authoritarian control

options.text: A one-party state, because the opposition contests no seats.
options.misconception: ignores the opposition seats recorded in the minutes

options.text: A two-party system, because only two blocs appear to matter.
options.misconception: counts blocs as parties when naming the party system

questions.explanation: One party leading while genuine rivals contest freely and win seats is the classic dominant-party pattern. A winning streak alone is not authoritarianism, and counting blocs as parties mislabels the system.
questions.hint: Ask whether rivals remain free to compete.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess how electoral rules shape party fragmentation
questions.stem: A briefing asks why adding a legal threshold to a proportional list system usually reduces the number of visible parties.

options.text: Because a threshold raises the number of seats each party receives.
options.misconception: reverses the effect of a threshold on seat totals

options.text: Because a threshold changes how votes are cast in each district.
options.misconception: confuses a national threshold with a district rule

options.text: Because a threshold removes the smallest parties from seat allocation.
Because a threshold forces all parties to merge before the election.
options.misconception: invents a compulsory merger that no threshold imposes

questions.explanation: A threshold excludes parties below the stated share from seat allocation, so the smallest parties disappear from the chamber and the effective number of parties falls. It does not enlarge entitlements or force mergers.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define civil society and distinguish it from the state
questions.stem: The civic note must explain why civil society is useful as a description of groups that are neither state nor market.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that the phrase marks the space of organised groups that stand between the state and the market, such as associations, charities, trade unions and professional bodies, and that it is useful precisely because it does not judge them. A group can contribute to public life by monitoring hospitals, running services or mobilising voters without being a party, a business or a public authority, and the label lets analysts discuss that contribution without implying any particular verdict on the group's influence. The note should add that the category is broad, and that a group operating inside the state or the market may sit at its edges rather than neatly inside it.

questions.explanation: Civil society names the space of organised groups between state and market, and it is useful because it describes rather than judges. Membership of that space can vary in how independent a group actually is.
questions.hint: Ask what the term is for, beyond judgement.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish political parties from other organised groups
questions.stem: A note describes a group that nominates candidates in local elections, publishes a programme and campaigns for seats.

options.text: It is civil society, because it is a non-governmental organisation.
options.misconception: confuses party organisation with non-governmental status

options.text: It is a pressure group, because it campaigns rather than governs.
options.misconception: treats campaigning as evidence against being a party

options.text: It is a social movement, because it mobilises supporters.
options.misconception: labels any mobilising group as a social movement

options.text: It is a political party, because it contests elections to seek office.

questions.explanation: Contesting elections, nominating candidates and seeking seats are the defining activities of a political party. Being a non-governmental organisation does not exclude that, and campaigning is exactly what parties do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the winner under a plurality rule

stimulus.body: The case note describes a district election in which the leading candidate received twenty-eight percent of the vote, the second candidate twenty-six percent, and the remaining votes were split among five others. The note records that no candidate reached fifty percent and that the leading candidate was duly returned.

questions.stem: Which reading of the district result in the case note is correct?

options.text: The result is void, because no candidate reached a majority of votes.
options.misconception: applies a majority threshold to a plurality contest

options.text: The result is void, because the margin over the second candidate was narrow.
options.misconception: treats a narrow plurality margin as voiding the result

options.text: The result was decided by a second round between the top two candidates.
options.misconception: invents a second round that the note does not mention

options.text: The seat was validly won under plurality by the leading candidate.

questions.explanation: Under plurality the highest vote-getter wins regardless of majority, so a twenty-eight percent leader validly takes the seat. Neither a majority requirement nor a runoff nor a minimum margin appears in the rule described.
questions.hint: Ask what rule produced the result.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how proportional allocation converts votes into seats
questions.stem: A clinic note explains that a party polling eleven percent of the vote in a region of two hundred seats receives twenty-two seats.

options.text: That is inconsistent, because eleven percent should give exactly twenty-two seats.
options.misconception: labels a matching entitlement as an inconsistency

options.text: That is inconsistent, because a party must poll over twenty percent to win seats.
options.misconception: invents a minimum vote share for gaining any seats

options.text: That is consistent, since twenty-two of two hundred seats matches eleven percent.
That is inconsistent, because only three parties may win seats.
options.misconception: invents a limit on the number of parties that can win

questions.explanation: Eleven percent of two hundred seats is exactly twenty-two, so the entitlement matches the vote share as proportional allocation requires. Neither a minimum vote level nor a cap on the number of parties is part of the rule.
questions.hint: Multiply the share by the seat total.

stimulus.body: The bulletin compares two districts. In the first, the winning party took thirty-four percent of the vote and the seat. In the second, the same party took nineteen percent of the vote and the seat. The bulletin comments that the two districts have identical numbers of registered voters and identical numbers of seats.

questions.stem: What does the bulletin indicate about how seat outcomes were produced?

options.text: The second district was counted differently from the first.
options.misconception: assumes a procedural irregularity rather than a rule effect

options.text: Both results are proportional, because vote share equals seat share.
options.misconception: calls a seat equal to a vote share proof of proportionality

options.text: The second result reflects a district system, where geography shapes outcomes.
The first result reflects a district system, where geography shapes outcomes.
options.misconception: attributes the seat-heavy result to the district rule

questions.explanation: In a district system a party can take a seat with a fifth of the vote if its support is concentrated there, so the second result points to geography deciding seats. A proportional system would not produce a nineteen percent vote with a full seat.
questions.hint: Ask what concentrates a party's votes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how governments are formed after a fragmented election
questions.stem: A ward business note records that the two largest parties together hold forty-four seats of one hundred.

options.text: Neither can govern alone, and together they still fall short of a majority.
They will govern together, because they are the two largest parties.
options.misconception: assumes the two largest parties can always govern together

options.text: The largest party will govern, because no other party will cooperate.
options.misconception: assumes cooperation is impossible without a majority

options.text: A third party must join the largest, since two parties are insufficient.
options.misconception: invents a rule requiring three partners regardless of arithmetic

questions.explanation: Forty-four seats is below the fifty needed for a majority, so the two parties together cannot govern and neither can govern alone. Larger parties or smaller ones would have to be brought in to reach the threshold.
questions.hint: Add the seats and compare with fifty.

In the following election the three small parties together polled twelve percent but were excluded, and the seat they had held was distributed to the parties that had cleared the threshold.

questions.stem: What does the clinic notice show about how the threshold rule works?

options.text: A threshold excludes small parties and their votes go to qualifying parties.
A threshold leaves excluded parties' votes outside the seat calculation.
options.misconception: assumes excluded votes simply disappear from the total

options.text: A threshold excludes small parties but voids the whole election result.
options.misconception: invents a nullification effect that the notice does not mention

options.text: A threshold requires small parties to merge before the election.
options.misconception: confuses the threshold with a merger requirement

questions.explanation: The notice shows excluded parties losing their seats and their votes going to parties that cleared the threshold, which is how such rules are normally built. The votes are redistributed under the formula rather than vanishing or voiding the election.
questions.hint: Follow what happened to the excluded votes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why plurality systems tend towards few effective parties
questions.stem: A reviewer argues that a proportional list system avoids the two-party squeeze because seats follow the national vote.

options.text: The argument holds, because proportional rules never reward concentration.
options.misconception: overstates the reach of proportional rules

options.text: The argument holds, because thresholds can never exclude the smallest parties.
options.misconception: overstates the protection that thresholds provide

options.text: The argument is partly right, but thresholds can reintroduce the squeeze.
The argument is wrong, because both systems always yield two parties.
options.misconception: ignores the difference between the two rules entirely

questions.explanation: Proportional allocation does remove the need for concentrated support, but a high threshold can exclude small parties and push voters toward the survivors. The argument captures the first effect while missing the second.
questions.hint: Weigh the rule against the threshold.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of a dominant-party system
questions.stem: Another note describes a system where one party wins most seats, several others compete for the rest, and the parties rotate as partners in government.

options.text: A two-party system, because only two blocs contest the vote.
options.misconception: counts governing partners as if they were the electoral competition

options.text: A one-party system, because the largest party dominates the chamber.
options.misconception: treats a large seat share as the absence of other parties

options.text: A minor-party system, because the smaller parties hold the balance.
options.misconception: names the arrangement by who holds the balance of power

options.text: A dominant-party system, with smaller parties as partners in government.

questions.explanation: A dominant-party system is one in which one party leads the electoral contest while smaller parties remain relevant, often as governing partners. Their presence as partners is what separates it from a one-party system.
questions.hint: Ask who leads and who partners.

questions.learningObjective: Assess how electoral rules shape party fragmentation

stimulus.body: The bulletin describes an electoral system that elects one member per district by first past the post. It notes that three parties have contested every district for decades, that the third party has won few seats because its support is spread thinly, and that the two larger parties have each concentrated their voters in particular regions.

questions.stem: What does the bulletin indicate about how the rules shaped the party system?

options.text: The three parties were equally successful because the rules were neutral.
options.misconception: ignores the concentrated support the bulletin records

options.text: The rules rewarded concentration, so the third party won few seats.
The third party failed because its voters were less politically active.
options.misconception: substitutes a voter quality explanation for the rule effect

options.text: The rules caused voters to spread evenly across both large parties.
options.misconception: claims the rule spread support rather than rewarding it

questions.explanation: First past the post rewards concentrated support, so the third party won few seats while the two larger parties prospered. The pattern follows from the rule rather than from differences in voter activity.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule rewarded here.

questions.learningObjective: Define civil society and distinguish it from the state
questions.stem: An outreach note describes a neighbourhood group that organises community meetings and is neither elected nor a registered business.

options.text: It is a political party, because it organises meetings on public issues.
options.misconception: equates community organising with electoral organisation

options.text: It is civil society, being an organised group outside state and market.
It is a government body, because it works with the council.
options.misconception: treats cooperation with officials as official status

options.text: It is a business, because it sells services to the council.
options.misconception: assumes paid services where the note records none

questions.explanation: An organised group that is neither elected nor commercial sits in the space that civil society names. Organising meetings is a typical civil society activity, and working with officials does not make a group part of the state.
questions.hint: Ask whether it is elected or commercial.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish political parties from other organised groups
questions.stem: The note must explain how a political party differs from a pressure group that campaigns on the same issues.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that the decisive difference is what the organisation is trying to achieve. A pressure group wants a particular policy outcome and works through publicity, campaigns and sometimes protest, and it accepts that other parties may hold office. A political party wants to hold office itself, so it nominates candidates, presents a programme covering the range of government and takes responsibility for governing or for the opposition. The note should add that the two can overlap in practice, since parties campaign on issues and pressure groups sometimes grow into parties, but the intended end point remains the distinguishing test, and membership figures or the volume of campaigning are not.

questions.explanation: Pressure groups pursue a policy outcome and leave office to others, while parties seek office and carry responsibility for governing. Overlaps occur, but the intended end point is what distinguishes them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the group wants to hold office.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the winner under a plurality rule
questions.stem: An intake note mentions a district where three candidates tied on the highest vote share.

options.text: A tie cannot be resolved by plurality alone, so a further rule applies.
The candidate listed first on the ballot takes the seat automatically.
options.misconception: invents a ballot-order tiebreak with no stated rule

options.text: The seat is awarded to the candidate with the most party members.
options.misconception: resolves the tie by membership rather than by votes

options.text: The seat is left unfilled until a fresh election is held.
options.misconception: assumes a vacancy is the automatic consequence of a tie

questions.explanation: Plurality ranks candidates by votes and says nothing about a tie, so a further rule such as a run-off or a lottery is needed. Ballot order and party membership are not part of the rule described.
questions.hint: Ask how the rule handles an equal ranking.

options.text: The system is a district system, because candidates were chosen by committee.
options.misconception: confuses candidate selection with the seat allocation rule

options.text: The system is a majoritarian system, because one list dominates the vote.
options.misconception: describes a proportional system as majoritarian without basis

options.text: The system is a threshold system, because remainders decide the last seats.
options.misconception: mistakes the remainder step for the exclusion rule

options.text: The system is proportional, with remainders deciding the final places.

questions.explanation: A fixed chamber of two hundred seats filled from one regional list, with seat shares close to vote shares, is proportional allocation. Remainders decide the last places, a step within the rule rather than a threshold or district feature.
questions.hint: Identify the allocation basis in the minutes.

questions.stem: A clinician wonders whether a chamber where the largest party holds forty-four seats on forty-four percent of the vote is proportionate.

No, because a party needs more than half the vote to be proportionate.
options.misconception: requires a vote majority as a condition of proportionality

options.text: No, because proportionality requires every party to have equal seats.
options.misconception: confuses proportionality with equality between parties

options.text: No, because a seat share above forty percent is always a distortion.
options.misconception: treats a large seat share as automatically distorting

questions.explanation: A seat share of forty-four alongside a vote share of forty-four is close to proportionality on these figures, even though the party is the largest. Proportionality compares the two shares rather than asking who won how many.
questions.hint: Compare the seat share with the vote share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how governments are formed after a fragmented election
questions.stem: Another civic note must explain why a fragmented election can produce a government that no voter had chosen as a package.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that with proportional rules the count determines who holds how many seats, and the government is then assembled afterwards from those seats. If no party has a majority, the parties that need each other must negotiate an agreement, and the combination that emerges is decided by the arithmetic of the chamber and by the bargaining strength of each party rather than by any list on a ballot. The note should add that the terms of such agreements may cover only a few subjects, leaving other policy areas to be handled without a mandate, which is why the resulting government can differ sharply from what any party's programme promised.

questions.explanation: Seats are fixed by the count and the government is assembled afterwards by negotiation, so the combination emerges from bargaining rather than from a ballot. Programme commitments may be diluted in the deal.
questions.hint: Ask when the governing combination is chosen.

questions.stem: A clinic letter explains that a party polling six percent is excluded where the threshold is five percent and a separate rule excludes any party below three.

options.text: The party is included, because it clears the main threshold of five percent.
options.misconception: ignores the stricter of the two applicable limits

options.text: The party is included, because six percent is larger than three percent.
options.misconception: treats the lower limit as if it were the binding one

options.text: The party is excluded, because thresholds apply to vote totals only.
options.misconception: claims thresholds apply to something other than vote share

options.text: The party is included, since it clears the higher of the two limits.

questions.explanation: Where two thresholds apply, the higher one governs, so a party at six percent clears both limits and keeps its seats. Reading only the five percent rule or only the three percent rule would give the wrong result.
questions.hint: Apply the stricter of the two limits.

options.misconception: describes the pattern incorrectly as having no local presence

options.text: Because the national result is calculated before district results are counted.
options.misconception: invents an order of counting that does not exist

options.text: Because a national vote share caps the number of seats a party may win.
options.misconception: confuses a seat cap with the district effect

questions.explanation: A district system rewards whoever finishes first in a district, so evenly spread support fails to produce first places anywhere and the party wins few seats. The effect comes from the geographic concentration of rival votes, not from any cap.

options.misconception: ignores the genuine opposition parties in such systems

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess how electoral rules shape party fragmentation
questions.stem: The note must explain why comparing two democracies by counting their parties can be misleading.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that a raw party count mixes together several different things. Two parties might sit inside one electoral coalition, or a single party might be a loose alliance of regional organisations that would count as several parties in a different system, and small parties that never cross a threshold may exist in the country without holding a seat. The count also depends on the unit of analysis, since a party that wins seats everywhere is politically different from one that wins a handful of seats in a single region. A careful comparison therefore reports how many parties win seats, how many are viable in practice and how the electoral rule shapes both, rather than quoting a single number.

questions.explanation: Raw party counts mix coalitions, loose alliances and excluded small parties, and the count depends on the unit of analysis. A comparison should report seat-winning and viable parties under each rule instead of a single number.
questions.hint: Ask what the count is counting.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why plurality systems tend towards few effective parties

stimulus.body: The note explains that in the survey country's district elections the two main parties between them took ninety-one percent of the seats, while three other parties contested every district and won nine seats between them. It adds that the districts are drawn so that no party can hold more than a fixed share of any one region.

questions.stem: What does the note indicate about the party system of the survey country?

options.text: The country uses a proportional system, since seats follow votes.
options.misconception: reads seat concentration as evidence of proportional allocation

options.text: The country uses a threshold, since small parties win few seats.
options.misconception: invents a threshold that the note does not mention

options.text: The country is a dominant-party system, since one party leads everywhere.
options.misconception: applies the dominant-party label without evidence of one party

options.text: The country shows a two-party tendency produced by district rules.

questions.explanation: Two parties taking ninety-one percent of seats while three others win nine points to the two-party squeeze produced by plurality districts. Seat concentration is not evidence of proportionality, and no single party is shown to lead everywhere.
questions.hint: Ask which rule produced that seat pattern.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how governments are formed after a fragmented election
questions.stem: A ward note records a chamber where the largest party holds thirty-eight seats and a two-party bloc holds thirty-one.

options.text: The largest party governs alone, because it has the most seats.
options.misconception: assumes the largest party may govern without a majority

options.text: Neither side governs alone, because the largest is short of a majority.
The two-party bloc governs, because it holds more seats than the largest.
options.misconception: ignores that thirty-one seats is also short of a majority

options.text: A fresh election is required, because no group holds a majority.
options.misconception: assumes a repeat poll is required after a fragmented result

questions.explanation: Neither thirty-eight nor thirty-one reaches the fifty needed for a majority, so neither side can govern alone and some agreement between them is required. The largest party leads the bargaining without being able to govern on its own.
questions.hint: Check each side against the majority mark.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an electoral threshold
questions.stem: A short policy note defines a legal threshold as a minimum vote share required to win seats.

options.text: A maximum vote share beyond which a party loses its seats.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the threshold effect

options.text: A rule that requires voters to approve a list by a set percentage.
options.misconception: confuses a seat threshold with a referendum quorum

options.text: A minimum vote share below which a party is excluded from seats.
A provision that increases the number of seats in small districts.
options.misconception: invents a seat redistribution rule

questions.explanation: A threshold is a floor below which a party gains no representation, which is why small parties are excluded from seats. It is not a ceiling, a vote approval rule or a mechanism for changing seat numbers.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the figure the rule cuts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of a dominant-party system
questions.stem: A review note describes a country where one party wins about forty percent of the vote and roughly half the seats, and three opposition parties contest freely.

options.text: A dominant-party system, in which one party leads without rivals being suppressed.
A two-party system, because only one challenger commands real support.
options.misconception: treats the absence of a strong runner-up as a two-party system

options.text: A single-party state, because one party holds the largest block of seats.
options.misconception: confuses a large block of seats with the absence of other parties

options.text: A hybrid regime, because the seat share exceeds the vote share.
options.misconception: reads a seat-vote difference as evidence of electoral unfairness

questions.explanation: One party leading the vote and the seat count while rivals contest freely is a dominant-party system, not a one-party state, since the opposition still wins seats. A seat-vote gap alone is not evidence of unfairness.
questions.hint: Ask whether the opposition still wins seats.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess how electoral rules shape party fragmentation
questions.stem: A policy team asks why electoral rules cannot be judged as more or less democratic simply by counting the parties they produce.

options.text: Because party counts are always reported incorrectly by the media.
options.misconception: dismisses party counts as data rather than as a measurement

options.text: Because the number of parties is fixed by the constitution in every case.
options.misconception: invents a constitutional fixation of the party count

options.text: Because different rules suit different purposes, and fragmentation is a design choice.
Because fewer parties always mean a more competitive electoral contest.
options.misconception: assumes fewer parties always means a more competitive contest

questions.explanation: Plurality concentrates and proportional allocation spreads, and both are legitimate design choices serving different purposes. A party count therefore measures the design rather than the quality of the contest.
questions.hint: Ask what a party count actually measures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define civil society and distinguish it from the state
questions.stem: The note must explain how a social movement differs from an established organisation such as a charity or a union.

answer.exemplar: The note should explain that the distinction is about organisation and orientation rather than about aims. A social movement is a loose, often temporary coalition that mobilises around a grievance or a proposed change in conduct, and it typically has no stable membership list, no elected officers and no permanent institution, so its strength is measured in participation and visibility. An established organisation has registered members, formal structures and continuity of existence, and it pursues its objectives through lobbying, litigation, service delivery or organisational pressure. A movement may harden into an organisation over time, and the same campaign can involve both, which is why the label describes the form of collective action rather than the cause being pursued.

questions.explanation: A movement is loose, temporary and mobilising, while an organisation has members, officers and continuity. The label describes the form of collective action rather than the cause pursued.
questions.hint: Compare structure with the cause pursued.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish political parties from other organised groups

stimulus.body: The closing note records that a local party association has run candidates in four elections, that it lost all of its seats at the last election, and that it has kept a formal membership and elected officers throughout. It adds that the association has now opened a national membership drive to contest more seats in the next cycle.

questions.stem: How should the association described in the closing note be classified?

options.text: It is no longer a party, because it won no seats at the last election.
options.misconception: treats election results as the test of party status

options.text: It is a pressure group, because it no longer holds elected office.
options.misconception: confuses holding office with being organised to seek it

options.text: It is civil society, because it has no representatives in the chamber.
options.misconception: confuses being unrepresented with being outside party politics

options.text: It is a political party, because it contests elections and seeks seats.

questions.explanation: Losing seats does not end a party's existence: the association still fields candidates and is preparing to contest more seats. Party status rests on contesting elections and seeking office, not on current representation.
questions.hint: Ask whether it still stands candidates.
